title: John 1:3-4: where does the sentence break at "that which has come to be"?
summary: The earliest manuscripts carry no punctuation. Ho gegonen ("what has come to be") can close v. 3 ("without him not one thing came to be that has come to be") or open v. 4 ("what has come to be, in him was life"). The choice changes whether life is predicated of creation or of the Word.

readings.label: Close v. 3 with ho gegonen: "not one thing that has come to be"
readings.rendering: without him not one thing came into being that has come into being. In him was life, and the life was the light of men
readings.grammar: Ho gegonen is a relative clause attached to oude hen; en autō zōē ēn begins a new sentence.
readings.modern: NA28, UBS and most modern translations (RSV, ESV, NIV)

fathers.work: Homilies on the Gospel of John
fathers.quote: For we will not put the full stop after not anything, as the heretics do.

readings.label: Stop after oude hen; v. 4 begins "what has come to be, in him was life"
readings.rendering: without him not one thing came into being. What has come to be in him was life, and the life was the light of men
readings.grammar: Ho gegonen is the subject of a new clause whose predicate is en autō zōē ēn.
readings.modern: Common in the second to fourth centuries; recorded as an alternative in NRSV margin

fathers.work: Tractates on the Gospel of John
fathers.quote: Because that which was made in Him was life; and before it was made there was life.
And what was made, in Him was life, and the life was the light of men.

macula_evidence: ὃ γέγονεν is parsed as a relative clause (<rel>) hanging off οὐδὲ ἕν, and John 1:4 opens with ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν as a new clause.

title: John 1:9 erchomenon: the light that comes, or every man who comes?
summary: Erchomenon can agree with phos ("the true light was coming into the world", a periphrastic ēn erchomenon) or with anthropon ("enlightens every man who comes into the world"). Both are grammatical.

readings.label: With anthropon: "every man coming into the world"
readings.rendering: the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world
readings.grammar: Accusative participle in agreement with πάντα ἄνθρωπον; cf. the rabbinic idiom "all who come into the world".

fathers.work: Homilies on the Gospel of John
fathers.quote: If He lights every man that comes into the world, how is it that so many continue unenlightened?
Immediately there appears the Word, that true light, which lights man on his coming into the world,

readings.label: With phos via ēn: "the true light was coming into the world"
readings.rendering: the true light, which enlightens everyone, was coming into the world
readings.grammar: Periphrastic imperfect ἦν ἐρχόμενον agreeing with φῶς, with ὃ φωτίζει πάντα ἄνθρωπον as a relative clause.

fathers.quote: The true light, which lightens every man, was coming into the world.

macula_evidence: ἦν[1] ... ἐρχόμενον[10] εἰς τὸν κόσμον is parsed as one clause (periphrastic 'was coming'), with ὃ φωτίζει πάντα ἄνθρωπον as a <rel> clause on τὸ φῶς.

title: John 1:18 monogenēs theos: adjective, or noun in apposition?
summary: On the reading monogenes theos (a separate textual question), the grammar is still open: monogenes may be an adjective ("the only-begotten God") or a substantive with theos in apposition ("the Unique One, God").

readings.label: Adjectival: "the only-begotten God"
readings.rendering: the only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father
readings.grammar: μονογενὴς modifies θεός as an attributive adjective.

fathers.quote: The only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him,
But the Only-begotten God, Who is in the bosom of the Father is excellent, and beyond all excellency

readings.label: Appositional: "the Unique One, God"
readings.rendering: the Unique One, who is God, who is in the bosom of the Father
readings.grammar: μονογενής is a substantivised adjective ("the unique one"); θεός stands in apposition to it.
readings.modern: NET ("the only one, himself God"); Wallace, GGBB 241-3

macula_evidence: μονογενὴς θεὸς is glossed 'one and only God' as a single noun group with ὁ ὤν as a <rel> clause.

title: John 5:39 eraunate: "Search" or "You search"?
summary: Eraunate is the same form in the present imperative and the present indicative. The imperative exhorts study of Scripture; the indicative observes that the audience already search it and still miss its testimony to Christ.

readings.label: Imperative: "Search the Scriptures"
readings.rendering: Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life
readings.grammar: Second-person plural present imperative, with ὅτι giving the reason for the command.

fathers.work: Homilies on the Gospel of John
fathers.quote: He said not, Read the Scriptures, but, Search the Scriptures.

readings.label: Indicative: "You search the Scriptures"
readings.rendering: You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life, yet it is they that testify of me
readings.grammar: Second-person plural present indicative; the following καὶ links the statement to the rebuke "you will not come to me".
readings.modern: Cyril of Alexandria; Westcott; NEB margin

fathers.quote: We will then, looking to what is more profitable and agreeable to what preceded, read it not imperatively, but rather as in connection and with a comma.

macula_evidence: Ἐραυνᾶτε τὰς γραφάς is the main clause with ὅτι as an <adv> reason clause, treated as an imperative.

title: John 7:37-38: whose belly, and what does "as the Scripture said" modify?
summary: No punctuation marks where "let him drink" ends. Either ho pisteuon begins a new sentence ("He who believes in me, as Scripture said, out of his belly...") with autou the believer, or it completes the invitation ("let him drink who believes in me") and autou refers to Christ. A third option keeps the believer's belly but attaches "as Scripture said" back to the believing.

readings.label: Believer's belly; "as Scripture said" introduces the quotation
readings.rendering: Let him who is thirsty come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as Scripture said, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water
readings.grammar: Ὁ πιστεύων is a nominative pendens resumed by αὐτοῦ (the believer); καθὼς εἶπεν ἡ γραφή points forward to the rivers saying.

fathers.work: Tractates on the Gospel of John
fathers.quote: There is therefore an inner thirst and an inner belly, because there is an inner man.

readings.label: Believer's belly; "as Scripture said" belongs to "believes in me"
readings.rendering: He who believes in me, as Scripture said: rivers of living water will flow out of his belly (Christ's own word, not a Scripture quotation)
readings.grammar: Stop after εἶπεν ἡ γραφή: the clause ποταμοὶ ... ῥεύσουσιν is an assertion of Christ.

fathers.work: Homilies on the Gospel of John
fathers.quote: Here we must place a stop, so that the, rivers shall flow from his belly, may be an assertion of Christ.

readings.label: Christ's belly: the believer drinks, and the rivers flow from Christ
readings.rendering: Let him who is thirsty come to me, and let him who believes in me drink. As Scripture said, out of his [Christ's] belly will flow rivers of living water
readings.grammar: Ὁ πιστεύων is the subject of πινέτω; αὐτοῦ refers to the speaker.
readings.modern: NRSV margin; Brown, Gospel of John (AB) 1.320-4

macula_evidence: Tree: ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμέ and the καθὼς clause are siblings before the main clause ποταμοὶ ... ῥεύσουσιν, with αὐτοῦ resumptive; it parses v. 38 as a new sentence but does not decide the referent of αὐτοῦ.

title: John 8:25 tēn archēn ho ti kai lalō: three ways to read it
summary: Ten archen can be a predicate ("[I am] the Beginning"), an adverbial accusative ("from the beginning", i.e. "what I have been telling you from the beginning") or part of a question ("why do I speak to you at all?"). Each yields a different answer to "Who are you?"

readings.label: Predicate: "[I am] the Beginning"
readings.rendering: The Beginning, which I also say to you
readings.grammar: Τὴν ἀρχήν as accusative predicate with an understood 'I am', and ὅ τι καὶ λαλῶ as a relative clause.
readings.modern: Vulgate (principium qui et loquor vobis), Douay-Rheims

fathers.work: Tractates on the Gospel of John
fathers.quote: Believe me [to be] the beginning, that you may not die in your sins.

readings.label: Adverbial: "from the beginning"
readings.rendering: What I have been telling you from the beginning
readings.grammar: Τὴν ἀρχήν as adverbial accusative ("at all, from the start") with ὅ τι as 'what'.

fathers.work: Homilies on the Gospel of John
fathers.quote: What then says Christ? The same that I told you from the beginning.

readings.label: Interrogative: "Why do I speak to you at all?"
readings.rendering: Why am I even speaking to you at all?
readings.grammar: Ὅ τι read as interrogative, with τὴν ἀρχήν meaning "at all" in a rhetorical question.
readings.modern: NRSV ("Why do I speak to you at all?")

macula_evidence: τὴν ἀρχήν sits inside a <rel> clause 'what the beginning also saying you', treated as adverbial accusative rather than as a predicate nominal.

title: John 9:3-4: does the purpose clause end the sentence or begin the next?
summary: "But that the works of God might be displayed in him" is elliptical. It may end Jesus' answer (with 9:4 a new sentence, "We must work...") or stand as the purpose of 9:4 ("so that the works of God might be displayed in him, we must work the works of him who sent me"). The difference is whether the blindness was ordained for display, or whether the display is the aim of the disciples' working.

readings.label: Full stop after "in him"
readings.rendering: Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but [he was born blind] so that the works of God might be displayed in him. We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day
readings.grammar: Ἀλλ' ἵνα φανερωθῇ is an elliptical clause completing v. 3; v. 4 opens with δεῖ.

readings.label: Comma after "in him": the clause goes with v. 4
readings.rendering: Neither this man nor his parents sinned. But so that the works of God might be displayed in him, we must work the works of him who sent me while it is day
readings.grammar: Ἵνα φανερωθῇ gives the purpose of δεῖ ἡμᾶς ἐργάζεσθαι in v. 4.
readings.modern: Noted by some commentators and in margins

macula_evidence: 9:3 ends with the ἵνα clause under ἀπεκρίθη, and 9:4 starts a separate clause with δεῖ ... <s> ἡμᾶς ἐργάζεσθαι.

title: John 14:1 pisteuete ... pisteuete: imperatives or indicatives?
summary: Pisteuete is identical in the present indicative and imperative, so the verse can read as two commands, two statements, or a statement and a command. Each shifts how Jesus' words to the troubled disciples are heard.

readings.label: Two imperatives
readings.rendering: Believe in God; believe also in me
readings.grammar: Both πιστεύετε are present imperatives, continuing the μὴ ταρασσέσθω command.

fathers.quote: Take as an instance the command, Believe in God, and believe also in Me.

readings.label: Indicative, then imperative
readings.rendering: You believe in God; believe also in me
readings.grammar: First πιστεύετε indicative (a premise), second imperative (the conclusion).
readings.modern: Vulgate (creditis ... et in me credite), Douay-Rheims

fathers.work: Homilies on the Gospel of John
fathers.quote: Anyhow, conversing with the disciples, He did speak thus: You believe in the Father, believe also on Me

readings.label: Two indicatives
readings.rendering: You believe in God, and you believe in me
readings.grammar: Both πιστεύετε are present indicatives, a statement of their existing faith offered as the ground for calm.

macula_evidence: The tree displays the two πιστεύετε clauses as coordinate main clauses without encoding mood.

title: John 19:35 ekeinos oiden: who is "that one"?
summary: Ekeinos ("that one") normally points away from the subject. It can mean the eyewitness himself (speaking of himself in the third person) or another person, whether Jesus or God, who guarantees the testimony.

readings.label: The eyewitness himself
readings.rendering: and he [the eyewitness] knows that he tells the truth, that you also may believe
readings.grammar: Ἐκεῖνος is used of the eyewitness as a solemn self-reference rather than of a different person.

fathers.work: Tractates on the Gospel of John
fathers.quote: for he knows who has seen, that he who has not seen might believe his testimony.

readings.label: Another person: Christ or God as guarantor
readings.rendering: and that One [Christ, or God] knows that he [the witness] speaks the truth
readings.grammar: Ἐκεῖνος points to a third party, since it normally contrasts with the previous subject.

macula_evidence: ἐκεῖνος[12] is the subject of οἶδεν with an ὅτι-clause object; the tree gives no referent.

title: John 20:17 mē mou haptou: "stop clinging" or "do not touch"?
summary: Mē + present imperative (haptou) can be read as a command to stop an action already begun ("stop clinging to me"), or as a general prohibition ("do not touch me"). The explanatory gar ("for I have not yet ascended") is then the reason Mary need not hold on, or the reason contact is refused.

readings.label: Stop clinging
readings.rendering: Stop clinging to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father
readings.grammar: Μὴ + present imperative of ἅπτομαι (middle), here "cling to", marks an action under way (Wallace, GGBB 724).
readings.modern: NIV ("Do not hold on to me"), NET

readings.label: Do not touch me
readings.rendering: Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father
readings.grammar: Μὴ + present imperative as a general prohibition with ἅπτομαι "touch".

macula_evidence: Tree glosses ἅπτου as 'cling to' but does not mark the aspect distinction; neutral on the grammatical reading.

title: John 20:23 apheontai / kekratēntai: "are forgiven" or "have been forgiven"?
summary: Apheontai and kekratentai are perfect passives. Read as a perfect of resulting state, forgiveness follows the apostles' act of forgiving or retaining. Read as a true perfect, the main clauses state a prior divine act ("they have already been forgiven") that the disciples declare.

readings.label: Result: forgiveness follows the apostles' act
readings.rendering: if you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven them; if you retain anyone's, they are retained
readings.grammar: Perfect passive as a state resulting from the aorist subjunctive ἀφῆτε in an ἂν-clause.

readings.label: Declarative: it has already been done in heaven
readings.rendering: if you forgive anyone's sins, they have already been forgiven; if you retain anyone's, they have already been retained
readings.grammar: Perfect denotes completed prior action; the apostles announce what God has already done.

macula_evidence: The tree places ἀφέωνται and κεκράτηνται as main clauses after ἄν-subjunctive adverbial clauses and does not encode tense force.

title: John 21:15 pleon touton: more than whom or what?
summary: Touton is a genitive of comparison, masculine or neuter. "More than these" can mean "more than these others love me" (subject comparison), "more than you love these men" (object comparison) or "more than you love these things" (boats, nets, fishing).

readings.label: More than the other disciples love me
readings.rendering: Do you love me more than these others do?
readings.grammar: Τούτων as masculine genitive of comparison, with the other disciples as subject of the understood verb.

fathers.quote: that is, Do you love Me more than these here do? He was speaking of the other disciples;

readings.label: More than you love the other disciples
readings.rendering: Do you love me more than you love these men?
readings.grammar: Τούτων as masculine genitive of comparison, with the disciples as object of the understood verb.

readings.label: More than you love these things
readings.rendering: Do you love me more than you love these things (boats, nets, fish)?
readings.grammar: Τούτων as neuter genitive of comparison, pointing at the fishing gear and catch.
readings.modern: Some commentators; noted in several translations

macula_evidence: The tree gives ἀγαπᾷς με πλέον τούτων flat with no referent for τούτων.

title: John 8:44 kai ho patēr autou: "the father of it" or "his father"?
summary: Autou may be neuter ("of the lie", so the devil is the father of falsehood) or masculine ("of him", the liar's father also called a liar). Gnostic and Manichaean readers used the second to posit a father of the devil.

readings.label: "The father of the lie"
readings.rendering: he is a liar and the father of it [falsehood]
readings.grammar: Αὐτοῦ refers back to τὸ ψεῦδος (neuter).
readings.modern: Nearly all modern translations (RSV, NIV, ESV, NAB)

fathers.work: Tractates on the Gospel of John
fathers.quote: and therefore he is the father of a lie, as God is the Father of the truth.

readings.label: "His father" (the devil's father)
readings.rendering: he is a liar and so is his father
readings.grammar: Αὐτοῦ read as masculine, referring to the liar, with ὁ πατήρ as a second subject.
readings.modern: KJV margin; Gnostic and Manichaean readers

macula_evidence: The tree glosses the final αὐτοῦ as 'it' (neuter, ψεῦδος), 'and the father it'.

title: Luke 1:35 to gennōmenon hagion: "the holy child" or "called holy"?
summary: Hagion may be an attributive adjective on to gennomenon ("the holy thing born will be called Son of God") or a predicate adjective of klethesetai ("the one born will be called holy, Son of God"). Each changes which title belongs to Jesus.

readings.label: Attributive: "the holy offspring will be called Son of God"
readings.rendering: therefore the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God
readings.grammar: Ἅγιον modifies τὸ γεννώμενον; υἱὸς θεοῦ is the predicate of κληθήσεται.
readings.modern: Vulgate (quod nascetur sanctum), RSV, NIV, ESV, NAB

fathers.quote: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God;

readings.label: Predicate: "will be called holy, the Son of God"
readings.rendering: therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God
readings.grammar: Ἅγιον is the predicate of κληθήσεται, with υἱὸς θεοῦ in apposition; gennomenon is a substantive.

macula_evidence: Tree gives τὸ γεννώμενον ἅγιον κληθήσεται υἱὸς θεοῦ as one flat clause without marking attributive versus predicate ἅγιον.

title: Luke 2:2 prōtē: "first census" or "census before Quirinius"?
summary: Prote can be an ordinal ("this was the first census, while Quirinius was governing") or a comparative of priority taking a genitive ("this census took place before Quirinius governed"). The second reading removes the apparent clash with Josephus, who dates Quirinius' census to AD 6.

readings.label: "This was the first census"
readings.rendering: This was the first registration, when Quirinius was governor of Syria
readings.grammar: Πρώτη as an ordinal agreeing with ἀπογραφή, contrasting this census with the later one (Acts 5:37).

readings.label: "Before Quirinius was governing"
readings.rendering: This registration took place before Quirinius was governor of Syria
readings.grammar: Πρώτη as a comparative of priority ("earlier than") with ἡγεμονεύοντος Κυρηνίου as a genitive of comparison.

macula_evidence: Tree gives πρώτη as a modifier within the main clause and the genitive absolute separately; it does not decide between ordinal and comparative.

title: Luke 2:14 anthrōpois eudokias: whose good will?
summary: Eudokias is a genitive that may express God's favour ("men of his good pleasure") or human good will ("men of good will"). The first makes peace a gift God bestows on those he favours; the second makes it depend on right disposition in men.

readings.label: God's favour: "men on whom his favour rests"
readings.rendering: on earth peace among men with whom he is pleased
readings.grammar: Genitive of source/possessor (Semitic 'men of his good pleasure'), with εὐδοκία as God's gracious choice.

fathers.quote: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among men of His good pleasure

readings.label: Human good will: "men of good will"
readings.rendering: on earth peace to men of good will
readings.grammar: Genitive of quality: εὐδοκία as the men's own right disposition (Vulgate hominibus bonae voluntatis).

fathers.quote: Said the Angels, Peace on earth unto rich men? No, but, Peace on earth unto men of a good will.

macula_evidence: Tree shows ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκίας as one phrase ('among men pleased') without distinguishing subjective from objective genitive.

title: Luke 2:49 en tois tou patros mou: "in my Father's house" or "about my Father's affairs"?
summary: Ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου has a neuter plural article with a genitive and no noun. It can be read as "in the places of my Father" (house) or "among the things of my Father" (business or affairs). Both make Jesus claim a unique relation to God as Father.

readings.label: In my Father's house
readings.rendering: Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?
readings.grammar: Neuter plural article + genitive as ellipsis for 'places', 'house'.

fathers.quote: but shall believe Christ, who says concerning the temple, Did you not know that I must be in My Father's house

readings.label: About my Father's business
readings.rendering: Did you not know that I must be about my Father's affairs?
readings.grammar: Neuter plural article + genitive as 'the things of', with ἐν meaning 'in the sphere of'.

macula_evidence: Tree renders ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου as 'in the of the father's my' without supplying a noun.

title: Luke 7:47 hoti ēgapēsen polu: is her love the cause or the evidence of forgiveness?
summary: Hoti can be causal ("her sins are forgiven because she loved much") or evidential ("her sins are forgiven, as shown by the fact that she loved much"). The parable of the two debtors (vv. 41-43) and the closing clause ("he to whom little is forgiven loves little") are used for the second.

readings.label: Causal: love is the ground of forgiveness
readings.rendering: her many sins are forgiven because she loved much
readings.grammar: Ὅτι introduces the reason for ἀφέωνται; ἠγάπησεν is the cause of the forgiveness.

fathers.quote: Wherefore I say unto you, her sins which are many are forgiven, since she loved much.

readings.label: Evidential: love shows that she has been forgiven
readings.rendering: her many sins have been forgiven, as her great love shows
readings.grammar: Ὅτι as 'for' giving proof of a state: forgiveness is prior and love the visible response (cf. the parable).

fathers.quote: for he loves most, to whom most is forgiven.
To whom much is forgiven, the same loves much.

macula_evidence: The ὅτι clause is an <adv> on ἀφέωνται, glossed 'for'; the tree does not decide whether it is causal or evidential.

title: Luke 16:16 biazetai: middle or passive?
summary: Biazetai is middle/passive. As a middle it reads "everyone forces his way into it" (eagerly, even violently). As a passive it reads "everyone is pressed into it" or "it is violently treated" (cf. Matt 11:12). Neither form nor context settles which was meant.

readings.label: Middle: everyone presses eagerly into it
readings.rendering: everyone forces his way into it
readings.grammar: Middle voice of βιάζομαι with πᾶς ... εἰς αὐτήν as the subject entering with intensity.

fathers.quote: Whoever hears and loves the sacred message takes it by force.

readings.label: Passive: everyone is pressed into it
readings.rendering: everyone is pressed into it (by the preaching)
readings.grammar: Passive of βιάζομαι: the many are being urged or compelled by the proclamation.

macula_evidence: βιάζεται is glossed 'urgently pressed' with πᾶς εἰς αὐτήν as subject, consistent with a middle sense (everyone presses in).

title: Luke 18:11 pros heauton: "prayed with himself" or "stood by himself"?
summary: Pros heauton can attach to the participle ("standing by himself/apart") or to the finite verb ("prayed to/about/with himself"). The first stresses the Pharisee's separation from the tax collector; the second his self-directed prayer.

readings.label: With "prayed": praying to/with himself
readings.rendering: The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself
readings.grammar: Πρὸς ἑαυτόν modifies προσηύχετο, "in his heart" or "to himself".

readings.label: With "standing": standing apart by himself
readings.rendering: The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus
readings.grammar: Πρὸς ἑαυτόν modifies σταθείς, "by himself/apart".

macula_evidence: The tree puts σταθεὶς πρὸς ἑαυτὸν ταῦτα προσηύχετο in one clause without resolving whether πρὸς ἑαυτόν attaches to the participle or the finite verb.

title: Luke 22:20 ekchynnomenon: what is poured out, the cup or the blood?
summary: In the long text, ekchynnomenon is a neuter dative singular participle agreeing with poterion (cup), not with haimati (blood, also dative). It can be read as modifying the cup (by metonymy, its contents are poured out) or as logically modifying the blood despite the agreement.

readings.label: Modifies the cup (metonymy)
readings.rendering: This cup, which is poured out for you, is the new covenant in my blood
readings.grammar: Participle in agreement with τὸ ποτήριον; the container stands for its contents.

readings.label: Modifies the blood
readings.rendering: This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you
readings.grammar: Ἐκχυννόμενον belongs logically to τῷ αἵματι, irregularly agreeing with the other noun (a recognised solecism).

macula_evidence: The relative clause τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυννόμενον is attached under τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον in the tree, i.e. to the cup.

title: Luke 23:43 sēmeron: "I tell you today" or "today you will be"?
summary: No punctuation marks where the comma goes. "Today" may close the solemn introduction ("Amen I say to you today: you will be with me in Paradise") or begin the promise ("I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise"). The first removes the claim that the thief entered Paradise that day.

readings.label: "Today you will be with me in Paradise"
readings.rendering: Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise
readings.grammar: Σήμερον goes with ἔσῃ; ἀμήν σοι λέγω is a complete formula.

fathers.quote: At least we must avoid, and shun with the utmost horror, that wicked punctuation of the heretics, who, as they do not believe that Christ could be found in Paradise on the same day on which He descended into hell, thus punctuate Verily, I say unto you today, and making a stop apply you shall be with Me in Paradise

readings.label: "I say to you today: you will be with me in Paradise"
readings.rendering: Truly I say to you today, you will be with me in Paradise
readings.grammar: Σήμερον goes with λέγω, a Semitic idiom of solemn emphasis.

macula_evidence: σήμερον[7] μετ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ is parsed as one clause, separate from ἀμήν σοι λέγω.

title: Acts 2:38 eis aphesin: for forgiveness, or because of it?
summary: Eis can express purpose or result ("for", "unto" forgiveness) or a causal-referential sense ("with reference to", "because of"). The plural metanoesate and third-person singular baptistheto also leave open whether forgiveness is tied to repentance alone or to repentance and baptism together.

readings.label: Purpose/result: baptism is for the forgiveness of sins
readings.rendering: Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins
readings.grammar: Εἰς + accusative of purpose/goal, governing βαπτισθήτω (and μετανοήσατε).

fathers.work: Homilies on the Acts of the Apostles
fathers.quote: If you are to receive a gift, if baptism conveys remission, why delay?

readings.label: Causal/referential: baptized because of forgiveness already received
readings.rendering: Repent, and be baptized every one of you ... on the basis of the forgiveness of your sins
readings.grammar: Εἰς as 'on account of', 'with reference to', so baptism follows forgiveness.

readings.label: Forgiveness attaches to repentance; baptism is parenthetical
readings.rendering: Repent for forgiveness of your sins (and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ), and you will receive the Holy Spirit
readings.grammar: Μετανοήσατε and ὑμῶν are second-person plural, while βαπτισθήτω ἕκαστος is third-person singular; εἰς ἄφεσιν goes with the plural imperative.

macula_evidence: The tree puts μετανοήσατε and βαπτισθήτω ... εἰς ἄφεσιν in successive coordinate clauses with εἰς ἄφεσιν inside the baptism clause; it does not encode the force of εἰς.

title: Acts 9:7 akouontes tēs phōnēs: "heard the voice" or "heard the sound"?
summary: Akouo takes the genitive here and the accusative in 22:9 ("did not hear the voice"). One tradition reads the genitive as hearing the sound and the accusative as understanding the words, harmonising the accounts. Others hold both cases can mean simply "hear" and that 22:9 means they did not understand.

readings.label: Genitive = heard a sound; accusative = understood words
readings.rendering: They heard the sound (of a voice) but saw no one; in 22:9 they did not catch the words
readings.grammar: Akouo with genitive of the thing perceived (sound), accusative for content understood, a distinction held by some older grammarians.

readings.label: No distinction: they heard the voice; 22:9 means they did not understand
readings.rendering: They heard the voice (without understanding what was said)
readings.grammar: Akouo + genitive or accusative are interchangeable in Koine (BDF §173).

macula_evidence: The tree shows ἀκούοντες τῆς φωνῆς as an adverbial participle clause but does not encode a case-based distinction.

title: Acts 13:48 tetagmenoi: appointed by God, or disposed?
summary: Ēsan tetagmenoi is a periphrastic pluperfect passive/middle. As a passive ("appointed", "ordained") it points to God's prior assignment to eternal life; as a middle ("had disposed themselves") it describes the hearers' own readiness.

readings.label: Passive: appointed (by God) to eternal life
readings.rendering: as many as had been appointed to eternal life believed
readings.grammar: Periphrastic pluperfect passive of τάσσω with an implied divine agent.

fathers.quote: Who could be ordained to eternal life save by the gift of perseverance?

fathers.work: Homilies on the Acts of the Apostles
fathers.quote: i.e., set apart for God.

readings.label: Middle: had disposed themselves to eternal life
readings.rendering: as many as were disposed toward eternal life believed
readings.grammar: Middle (reflexive) sense: they had set themselves toward eternal life.

macula_evidence: τεταγμένοι is parsed with ἦσαν as 'were appointed' (passive) in the relative clause.

title: Acts 19:2 pisteusantes: "when" or "after" you believed?
summary: Elabete pisteusantes pairs two aorists. The participle may express action coincident with the main verb ("did you receive the Spirit when you believed?") or antecedent action ("after you believed"). The first implies reception at conversion; the second a distinct later reception.

readings.label: Coincident: "when you believed"
readings.rendering: Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?
readings.grammar: Aorist participle of attendant circumstance, coincident with the aorist ἐλάβετε.

readings.label: Antecedent: "after you believed"
readings.rendering: Did you receive the Holy Spirit after you believed?
readings.grammar: Aorist participle of antecedent action (the usual default before an aorist verb).
readings.modern: KJV ("since"); Pentecostal and some Catholic commentators

macula_evidence: The tree shows ἐλάβετε πιστεύσαντες as verb plus adverbial participle without tense-force labelling.

title: Acts 20:28 tou haimatos tou idiou: "his own blood" or "the blood of his Own"?
summary: Tou idiou with tou haimatos can be adjectival ("his own blood", so God purchased the church with his own blood) or substantive ("the blood of his Own [Son]", cf. Rom 8:32). The textual question theou/kyriou is separate.

readings.label: Adjectival: "through his own blood"
readings.rendering: the church of God, which he obtained through his own blood
readings.grammar: Ἰδίου as attributive adjective modifying αἵματος, with θεοῦ as antecedent (the blood of God).

fathers.quote: and what kind of price? The blood of God.

readings.label: Substantive: "through the blood of his Own [One]"
readings.rendering: the church of God, which he obtained through the blood of his Own
readings.grammar: Ὁ ἴδιος as a substantive ("the Own/Beloved"), paralleled by Rom 8:32; avoids saying God shed blood.
readings.modern: NET margin; Metzger, Textual Commentary on Acts 20:28

macula_evidence: τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ ἰδίου glossed 'with the blood the his own' with ἰδίου as a modifier of αἵματος (adjectival).
